lines.text: Ananya wants her own DSA tutor, not someone else's chatbot. All it takes is one short Python script.
Because every serious AI product starts the same way: with an API call.
First, a virtual environment, so this project's packages never break her other work.
Then two installs, and a small file called dot env, which holds her API key.
The call itself is an ordinary HTTPS request. Her code sends a model name and a list of messages.
A system message sets the rules: you are a patient DSA tutor. A user message carries her question.
The key rides along in a header, and the provider runs the model on its own servers.
Back comes the answer, plus two fields beginners skip: the finish reason, and the usage.
Stop means the model finished. Length means it was cut off. Usage counts the tokens she is billed for.
For a follow-up, her code sends the whole list again, because the model remembers nothing between calls.
One rule matters most. The key is a password. It lives in dot env, and dot env goes in git ignore.
If it ever leaks, deleting the commit is not enough. Revoke the key and create a new one.
So that is an API call: messages out, text and a token count back, and the key never touches your code.
Next lesson: prompt engineering that survives production.
